title: Epigenetic age and cardiometabolic disease in Guatemalan adults: a cross-sectional analysis
journal: Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition

sections.abstract:
Epigenetic clocks, biomarkers of aging, show older biological ages among individuals with cardiometabolic disease. Epigenetic age acceleration, often calculated as the residuals from regressing epigenetic age on chronological age, reflects when an individual’s biological age is older or younger than expected. Most clocks were developed and validated in Western populations. This study examined associations of epigenetic age acceleration with obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome among Guatemalan adults.

We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of data from participants in the Institute of Nutrition of Central America and Panama (INCAP) Nutritional Supplementation Trial Cohort. DNA methylation (DNAm) was assessed in buffy coat samples using the MethylationEPIC v2 array and standard quality control procedures. Epigenetic age was quantified using DunedinPACE, PhenoAge, and GrimAge. Linear regression models were used to assess associations of obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and metabolic syndrome with epigenetic age acceleration. Dependent variables were DunedinPACE values and PhenoAge and GrimAge residuals. Covariates included sex, birth year, and a clustering variable to account for sibships.

We analyzed data from 1,095 adults (mean age 45 y; 60.3% female; 73.3% overweight or obese; 37.8% with hypertension; 15.4% with diabetes; 66.9% with metabolic syndrome). DunedinPACE (mean 1.2, SD 0.1), PhenoAge (mean 46.7, SD 6.7) and GrimAge (mean 56.3, SD 4.1) all indicate accelerated biological aging. Pearson correlations among the clocks were ≥ 0.5. DunedinPACE and PhenoAge indicated age acceleration among women (DunedinPACE β = 0.04; 95% CI: 0.03, 0.05; PhenoAge β = 0.94; 95% CI: 0.28, 1.60) whereas GrimAge suggested age acceleration among men (β= − 1.02; 95% CI: − 1.31, − 0.72). All three clocks showed accelerated aging among individuals with diabetes (DunedinPACE β = 0.09; 95% CI: 0.07, 0.10; PhenoAge β = 2.69; 95% CI: 1.63, 3.74; GrimAge β = 1.18; 95% CI: 0.71, 1.65). DunedinPACE indicated a faster rate of aging across all cardiometabolic conditions examined, whereas the strength and consistency of associations for PhenoAge and GrimAge varied by condition.

We observed consistent associations of accelerated DunedinPACE with multiple cardiometabolic conditions. All epigenetic clocks showed associations of epigenetic age acceleration with diabetes. These findings emphasize the need for longitudinal analyses to determine the direction and causality of these relationships.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s41043-026-01255-4.

Keywords: Epigenetic age, Ageing, Developmental origins of adult disease
sections.introduction:
Global increases in life expectancy have led to a rising burden of age-related chronic diseases [ 1 ]. This shift is especially pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where rapid gains in longevity are outpacing the capacity of health and social systems to support aging populations [ 2 , 3 ]. These challenges are compounded by the ‘double burden’ of malnutrition, the coexistence of high prevalences of early-life undernutrition and adult overnutrition [ 4 ]. Early-life undernutrition increases the risk of cardiometabolic disease and accelerated biological aging later in life [ 5 , 6 ], while adult overnutrition, driven by urbanization, processed diets, and reduced physical activity, further exacerbates this risk. Together, these life-course nutritional exposures increase susceptibility to cardiometabolic disease [ 4 ].

Biological aging refers to the gradual decline in physiological function that typically accompanies chronological aging [ 7 ]. Unlike chronological age, which simply reflects chronological time since birth, biological age captures the cumulative impact of genetic, environmental, and behavioral factors on the body’s systems [ 7 ]. Epigenetic clocks are biomarkers based on DNA methylation (DNAm) patterns that provide a quantifiable measure of biological age, revealing differences between biological and chronological age and offering insights into individual variation in aging and disease risk across individuals with similar chronological ages [ 7 ].

Epigenetic clocks have largely been developed and validated in Western populations, and most research on biological age acceleration and cardiometabolic diseases has focused on high-income countries. Therefore, our understanding of associations between epigenetic age and cardiometabolic diseases may not reflect the experiences of more ancestrally diverse populations, or individuals living in LMICs. Guatemala provides a relevant setting to examine these relationships: historically marked by high rates of childhood undernutrition and stunting, the country is now experiencing rapid increases in adult overweight, obesity, and non-communicable diseases [ 4 , 8 , 9 ]. Furthermore, its population is largely admixed, with a combination of indigenous (primarily Maya) and European (mostly Spanish) ancestry [ 10 ].

In this study, we examined associations between cardiometabolic disease and biological aging in the Institute of Nutrition of Central America and Panama (INCAP) Nutritional Supplementation Trial Cohort (INSTC), a well-characterized cohort of Guatemalan adults. We hypothesized that individuals with cardiometabolic diseases would exhibit greater epigenetic age acceleration compared to those without these conditions.
sections.methods:
Four Guatemalan villages participated in a cluster-randomized nutrition supplementation trial conducted between 1969 and 1977 [ 11 ]. Villages were assigned to receive either “atole,” a protein- and energy-rich supplement, or “fresco,” a protein-free, lower-energy beverage. Both drinks had comparable micronutrient content and were freely available to all village residents. Supplement consumption was recorded for pregnant and lactating women and children up to age seven [ 11 ]. Comprehensive descriptions of the original trial methodology have been published elsewhere [ 11 , 12 ].

The original trial participants ( n = 2,392) have been followed into adulthood. This study utilizes data collected during the follow-up wave conducted from 2015 to 2017 [ 13 ]. Individuals were excluded if they were lost to follow-up, declined participation, or if they were pregnant or lactating at the time of assessment.

Data were collected at study clinics in the original study villages and at INCAP facilities in Guatemala City. Sociodemographic information was obtained through interviews and classified into socioeconomic status tertiles derived from principal component analysis of household characteristics and durable goods, as previously described [ 13 , 14 ]. A study clinician completed a medical examination, including assessments of anthropometry (height, weight) and blood pressure. Blood pressure was measured three times. If the systolic or diastolic readings differed by more than 10 mm Hg, a fourth measurement was taken, and the average of the two closest readings was used. When only three measurements were taken, the average of the second and third readings was used. Participants were offered a mixed-nutrient challenge if their fasting blood glucose was < 180 mg/dL and they did not have known diabetes. Details of the challenge have been previously published [ 15 , 16 ].

A trained phlebotomist drew fasting and 2-hour post-challenge venous blood samples and processed them into plasma, serum, and buffy coat aliquots [ 13 , 14 ]. All samples were placed on dry ice immediately after collection and moved to a − 20 °C freezer for temporary storage the same day. Samples remained at −20 °C until transported to a − 80 °C freezer the INCAP laboratory for long term storage. Samples were shipped to Emory University and remained in −80 °C freezers until DNA extraction.

Obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and metabolic syndrome were classified using similar criteria to those previously used in this cohort based on the 2025 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care, the 2025 American Heart Association guidelines, and the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III guidelines for Metabolic Syndrome [ 13 , 14 , 17 – 19 ]. Specifically, overweight was defined as a BMI ≥ 25.0 kg/m 2 and < 30.0 kg/m 2 , obesity was defined as a BMI ≥ 30.0 kg/m 2 . Prediabetes was based on the 2025 American Diabetes Association diagnostic criteria of fasting plasma glucose of 100–125 mg/dL, 2-h post-challenge glucose of 140–199 mg/dl, or HbA1c between 5.7 and 6.4% among participants not reporting use of diabetes medication. Diabetes was classified as a fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or greater, post-challenge glucose levels 200 mg/dL or greater, or HbA1c 6.5% or current use of diabetes medication. Elevated blood pressure was considered systolic blood pressure of 120–129 mm Hg and a diastolic blood pressure of less than 80 mm Hg among participants not using anti-hypertensive medication. Hypertension was considered a systolic blood pressure of 130 mm Hg or greater or a diastolic blood pressure of 80 mm Hg or greater, or current use of anti-hypertensive medication. Metabolic syndrome was defined as ≥ 3 of the following: waist circumference > 88 cm (women) or > 102 cm (men); fasting glucose ≥ 100 mg/dL or diabetes medication; triglycerides ≥ 150 mg/dL or statin use; HDL < 40 mg/dL (men) or < 50 mg/dL (women); blood pressure ≥ 130/85 mmHg or antihypertensive medication.

This study protocol received Institutional Review Board approval from Emory University (Atlanta, Georgia, USA), and the Institute of Nutrition of Central America and Panama (Guatemala City, Guatemala). Participants provided written informed consent in Spanish prior to data collection.

Genomic DNA was isolated from stored buffy coat samples using the Qiagen QiAmp DNA Mini Kit. DNA was first extracted using the Qiagen QIAcube Automated DNA/RNA Isolation and Purification System. The concentration of DNA in each sample was assessed using the Quant-iTTM PicoGreen ® double-stranded DNA assay. Samples with insufficient DNA concentration were manually re-extracted using the same Qiagen kit. All extractions were completed between August 2023 and March 2024.

To reduce potential batch and chip-related variation, samples were plated to randomly and evenly distribute participants from 12 exposure groups across each plate, row, and column. These groups were defined by supplement type (Atole or Fresco), exposure duration (full exposure during the first 1,000 days, partial exposure [1–999 days], or no exposure), and biological sex (male or female). DNA methylation profiling was performed on approximately 935,000 CpG sites using the Illumina Infinium™ MethylationEPIC v2.0 BeadChip [ 20 , 21 ]. Cell type proportions were estimated from the DNA methylation data using the IDOL algorithm [ 22 ] following the publicly available workflow: https://github.com/PGC-PTSD-EWAS/EPIC_QC .

DNA methylation pre-processing and quality control followed standard protocols for the EPIC v2.0 array as described by Pidsley et al. [ 23 ]. Quality control (QC) procedures aimed to (1) detect poor quality samples, (2) exclude underperforming CpG probes, and (3) reduce technical variation in methylation measurements. QC protocol incorporated processes from ewastools [ 24 , 25 ] and the Enmix pipeline [ 26 – 30 ]. The complete QC pipeline is available at: https://github.com/PGC-PTSD-EWAS/EPICv2_pipeline .

We estimated epigenetic age using three established second- and third-generation DNA methylation clocks: DunedinPACE, PhenoAge, and GrimAge [ 31 – 33 ]. The first-generation clocks, such as Horvath [ 34 , 35 ] and Hannum [ 36 ], were trained to estimate DNAm age based solely on chronological age. Newer clocks, including DunedinPACE, PhenoAge, and GrimAge, were trained on additional data beyond chronological age, including biomarkers and health outcomes. DunedinPACE estimates the current pace of biological aging [ 37 ], expressed as years of biological age accrued per chronological year, and was trained on longitudinal changes in 19 organ-system biomarkers measured over two decades in the Dunedin Cohort Study. PhenoAge estimates a composite measure called Phenotypic Age and was trained on chronological age, nine clinical biomarkers, and mortality risk [ 32 ]. GrimAge predicts time-to-death and healthspan, and was trained on chronological age, DNAm surrogates for 12 plasma proteins, and smoking history (pack-years) [ 38 ]. DunedinPACE is unique in capturing a rate of aging. PhenoAge and GrimAge estimate biological age, for which residuals - differences between estimated biological age and chronological age - are typically used in analyses. For descriptive purposes, we created a variable called DunedinAge, which expresses DunedinPACE as an age rather than a rate, allowing direct comparison with PhenoAge and GrimAge. DunedinAge was calculated by multiplying each participant’s DunedinPACE value by their chronological age.

Clock values were calculated with the DunedinPACE [ 31 ] and MethylCIPHER [ 32 , 38 , 39 ] R packages. While most epigenetic clocks were originally developed using data from prior versions of the array (typically the Infinium ® HumanMethylation450 BeadChip (450k array), our DNA methylation data were generated using the Infinium ® MethylationEPIC v2 950k array. This updated array provides broader coverage of the epigenome, however it does not include some of the CpG sites required for clock calculations [ 40 ]. We applied principal component–based adjustments [ 41 ] (using the PC-Clocks R package) to the PhenoAge and GrimAge clocks to minimize technical noise and improve consistency across methylation arrays. This is an established approach for harmonizing epigenetic clock estimates across platforms [ 40 ]. For the DunedinPACE clock, we imputed missing CpGs with mean β-values from the publicly available PhenoAge training dataset (GEO 40279) [ 36 ], since a principal component–adjusted version of DunedinPACE is not yet available.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the study population, with means and standard deviations reported for continuous variables and frequencies for categorical variables. We used mixed effect linear regression models to evaluate the associations between cardiometabolic diseases and biological aging. DunedinPACE was analyzed directly. To account for the correlation between epigenetic and chronological age, we regressed PhenoAge and GrimAge measure on chronological age and used the resulting residuals as the primary outcome in our models.

The base model covariates for these analyses include a binary variable for sex, a continuous variable for birth year, a binary dummy variable for n-1 levels of each cardiometabolic condition (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome) category. For example, the model for diabetes included a dummy variable for prediabetes (yes/no), and another dummy variable for diabetes (yes/no). Participants without the cardiometabolic condition (i.e. without prediabetes or diabetes) served as the reference group. Models also included a random effect for sibships (maternal ID). Hypertension and metabolic syndrome models additionally adjusted for height. These methods are consistent with our previous analyses assessing the impact of early-life nutrition on adult diabetes risk [ 13 ]. The primary model did not adjust for the original early-life nutritional intervention, which occurred nearly 40 years earlier and whose role as a potential confounder is uncertain; it was included only in sensitivity analyses. The primary model was as follows:

To account for multiple testing in the primary analyses, we considered three independent tests – epigenetic age with BMI, hypertension, and diabetes. Statistical significance for the primary analyses was therefore assessed using a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of α = 0.05 ÷ 3 = 0.0167.

We conducted several sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of our findings. First, we modeled cardiometabolic conditions as ordinal variables instead of binary dummy variables to examine whether associations with biological aging followed a stepwise pattern. Second, with cardiometabolic conditions modeled as binary dummy variables, we additionally adjusted for exposure to the original early-life nutrition intervention, given prior evidence linking this intervention to long-term cardiometabolic outcomes [ 13 , 14 ]. We then additionally adjusted for estimated blood cell type proportions (CD8 T cells, CD4 T cells, natural killer [NK], B cells, and monocytes) as variation in leukocyte composition can influence DNA methylation profiles and potentially confound associations with biological aging [ 42 ]. Cell type proportions sum to 100%, thus we excluded granulocytes from the model to avoid collinearity among all the cell-types) [ 42 ]. To address the potential confounding effects of education and smoking status we conducted a sensitivity analysis adjusting the main models for education (less than primary as the reference, primary, some secondary, secondary and more) and smoking status (never smoker as the reference, former smoker, current smoker). Lastly, we conducted sex stratified analyses to assess the magnitude and direction of associations of the main model among women and among men, however this study is underpowered to detect statistical significance of these associations. For all sensitivity analyses we report unadjusted p-values given that these models are considered exploratory.

All statistical analyses were conducted using R statistical software (version 4.4.1). Statistical significance was assessed at the conventional alpha level of 0.05.
sections.results:
We analyzed data from 1,113 participants (48% of the original 2,392 participants) who attended a clinical exam and had a DNA sample available for analysis (Fig. 1 ). 18 samples were excluded during the quality control process.

Participant flow diagram

The study sample ( n = 1095) had a mean age of 45 years (SD = 4.3). Most participants had only primary (34.5%) or less than primary (43.5%) education (Table 1 ). Approximately 20% lived in Guatemala City (Table 1 ). Over two-thirds of participants had overweight or obesity (73.3%), and a similar proportion had metabolic syndrome (66.9%). 15.4% of participants met the diagnostic criteria for diabetes and 37.8% for hypertension. The prevalence of all cardiometabolic diseases (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome) was higher among women than men (Table 1 ). Losses to follow-up were not related to exposure to the original trial intervention. Participants lost to follow-up in this wave were largely similar to those who remained in the study, although fewer males were retained [ 13 , 14 ]. Potential impacts of attrition have been previously evaluated and found not to meaningfully influence estimates [ 13 , 14 , 43 ].

DunedinPACE was higher among participants classified as overweight (β = 0.03; 95% CI: 0.01, 0.04) and obese (β = 0.06; 95% CI: 0.05, 0.08) (Table 2 ; Figs. 2 and 3 ) and in those with hypertension (β = 0.02; 95% CI: 0.002, 0.03) (Table 2 ; Figs. 2 and 3 ). However, the association with hypertension no longer statistically significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. All clocks were associated with accelerated biological aging among individuals classified with diabetes. DunedinPACE suggested individuals with diabetes were aging 9% (95% CI: 0.07, 0.10) faster (1.08 months) than participants without diabetes. PhenoAge residuals were 2.69 years higher (95% CI: 1.63, 3.74), and GrimAge residuals 1.18 years higher (95% CI: 0.71, 1.65) among participants with diabetes compared to those without (Table 2 ; Figs. 2 and 3 ). DunedinPACE (β = 0.05; 95% CI: 0.03, 0.06) and GrimAge residuals (β = 0.37; 95% CI: 0.03, 0.71), were also elevated among individuals meeting criteria for metabolic syndrome (Table 2 ; Figs. 2 and 3 ). However, the association of GrimAge with metabolic syndrome was no longer statistically significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.

Our findings were consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses. Effect directions were consistent when diseases (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, metabolic syndrome) were modeled ordinally (Supplemental Table 1 , Supplemental Figs. 1 –4), when the original intervention assignment was included as a covariate (Supplemental Table 2 , Supplemental Figs. 1 –4), with additional adjustment for both the original intervention assignment and cell-type proportions (Supplemental Table 3, Supplemental Figs. 1 –5), and with additional adjustment for education and smoking status (Supplemental Table 4, Supplemental Figs. 1 –5). Effect sizes for diabetes were slightly attenuated after adjusting for the intervention and further attenuated when adjusting for cell-type proportions (Supplemental Tables 2–3). DunedinPACE and GrimAge were significantly associated with metabolic syndrome in the main model (Table 2 ). These associations were no longer significant after adjusting for the intervention (Supplemental Table 2) but regained significance with additional adjustment for cell-type proportions (Supplemental Table 3). In each metabolic syndrome model, effect sizes were modestly reduced with the addition of covariates. When additionally adjusting for education and smoking status, DunedinPACE no longer remained significantly associated with hypertension at the uncorrected α = 0.05 level (Supplemental Table 4).

In sex-stratified analyses, DunedinPACE remained significantly accelerated among overweight women (β = 0.03; 95% CI: 0.01, 0.05), but not men (Supplemental Tables 5 and 6). Conversely, GrimAge was significantly negatively associated with overweight in men (β = − 0.71; 95% CI: − 1.27, − 0.15), but not in women. Prediabetes also remained significantly associated with accelerated DunedinPACE in women (β = 0.02; 95% CI: 0.002, 0.04), but not in men (Supplemental Tables 5 and 6). Diabetes remained robustly associated with accelerated aging across all three clocks in both sexes (Supplemental Tables 5 and 6). Effect sizes for diabetes were larger in men (DunedinPACE β = 0.10; PhenoAge β = 3.12; GrimAge β = 1.30) than in women (DunedinPACE β = 0.08; PhenoAge β = 2.47; GrimAge β = 1.18) (Supplemental Tables 5 and 6). Metabolic syndrome also remained significantly associated with DunedinPACE, with stronger effects in women (β = 0.05; 95% CI: 0.03, 0.07) than in men (β = 0.03; 95% CI: 0.02, 0.05). Some associations observed in pooled models did not persist after sex stratification (Supplemental Tables 5 and 6). The relationship between DunedinPACE and hypertension was no longer significant in women or men (Supplemental Tables 5 and 6), and GrimAge was no longer significantly associated with metabolic syndrome in either sex (Supplemental Tables 5 and 6). We note that our analyses are underpowered to formally test for effect modification by sex. These sex-stratified results are provided for descriptive purposes and to contextualize findings across men and women.
sections.discussion:
Participants in this study of the INSTC showed signs of accelerated biological aging based on three epigenetic clocks: DunedinPACE, PhenoAge, and GrimAge. Overall, accelerated epigenetic aging was most pronounced among women and among individuals with diabetes. One clock, DunedinPACE, indicated a faster rate of aging across all four cardiometabolic conditions (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, metabolic syndrome) examined. The strength and consistency of associations with cardiometabolic disease differed among the other clocks.

All three clocks indicated epigenetic age acceleration, with mean DunedinPACE of 1.2 (indicating faster aging), and mean PhenoAge and GrimAge exceeding mean chronological ages. Most epigenetic clocks were developed in Western populations, and few studies have systematically compared their performance across multi-ethnic groups. Horvath et al. examined intrinsic epigenetic age acceleration (cell-intrinsic aging independent of blood cell composition) and extrinsic epigenetic age acceleration (capturing immune-related aging in whole blood) in several multi-ethnic cohorts. They reported that Hispanics have lower intrinsic but higher extrinsic aging than Caucasians [ 44 ]. They also observed that Hispanics born outside the United States but living in the United States had higher intrinsic aging measures than Hispanics born in the United States [ 44 ]. These differences may relate to metabolic and inflammatory profiles and variations in immune cell composition that have been observed among Hispanic populations [ 44 – 47 ]. Our findings are generally consistent, showing higher aging in this Guatemalan cohort that is primarily Ladino (a culturally Hispanic group in Guatemala, primarily of mixed indigenous and Spanish ancestry) born and residing in Guatemala [ 10 ]. However, without systematic multi-ethnic comparisons, the role of ethnicity in aging cannot be fully assessed, highlighting the potential need to calibrate epigenetic clocks for non-Western populations.

The variation in the direction and strength of some associations may reflect differences in how each epigenetic clock was developed. First-generation clocks, such as Horvath [ 34 ] and Hannum [ 36 ], were trained to predict chronological age. In this study, we used two second-generation clocks (PhenoAge [ 32 ] and GrimAge [ 38 ]) and a third-generation clock (DunedinPACE [ 31 ]) that measures the rate of biological aging. These newer clocks were trained using a combination of chronological age, clinical biomarkers, and health-related outcomes. PhenoAge was trained to predict a composite phenotypic age derived from clinical biomarkers associated with morbidity and mortality, including markers of metabolic and inflammatory function [ 32 ]. GrimAge was developed using DNA methylation surrogates for plasma proteins and smoking pack-years to predict time to death [ 38 ]. DunedinPACE is unique in that it was trained on longitudinal changes in multiple cardiometabolic risk factors, including body mass index, waist-to-hip ratio, blood pressure, glycated hemoglobin, and several lipid measures from the Dunedin New Zealand birth cohort [ 37 ]. As a result, each clock may be sensitive to different biological pathways or disease processes, which could explain why associations with cardiometabolic disease appear more consistent for DunedinPACE compared with other clocks in this study [ 48 ]. Robust sensitivity analyses suggest that these observed associations likely reflect true underlying biological processes.

Diabetes was associated with accelerated aging across all clocks. Diabetes is consistently associated with acceleration in other studies among similar populations and likely reflects the systemic, multi-organ system impact of the disease [ 49 – 51 ]. A systematic review by Oblak et al. found consistent evidence that GrimAge and PhenoAge show accelerated epigenetic age in individuals with diabetes [ 48 ]. Although DunedinPACE was not included in that review, it has been shown to be accelerated in both prevalent and incident diabetes in the Melbourne Collaborative Cohort Study [ 50 ]. We used several blood-based biomarkers to classify diabetes status in addition to considering individuals who self-reported taking diabetes medication. This approach is especially important in LMICs, where limited screening infrastructure, medication availability, and chronic disease management often leave many individuals undiagnosed, untreated, or inconsistently treated [ 52 , 53 ]. Our analyses include individuals with both well-controlled and poorly controlled diabetes; however, gaps in care may amplify the biological impact of diabetes in this cohort.

Hypertension and cardiovascular disease have been linked to accelerated aging in previous studies [ 54 , 55 ]. In our cohort, hypertension was significantly associated only with DunedinPACE, while the other clocks showed inconsistent results. However, the association with DunedinPACE did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, suggesting that this finding should be interpreted cautiously. This variation may reflect differences in the biological pathways each clock captures. Measurement error could also play a role: although blood pressure was measured multiple times for each participant, these tests are inherently less precise than blood-based biomarkers. Oblak et al. reported consistent evidence of epigenetic age acceleration in individuals with cardiovascular disease using the Hannum, Horvath, Levine, and GrimAge clocks; however, their review included studies of cardiovascular outcomes beyond hypertension (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease) [ 48 ].

BMI-based categories of overweight and obesity were associated with accelerated aging as measured by DunedinPACE. PhenoAge showed positive associations with both overweight and obesity, while GrimAge was inversely associated with overweight but positively associated with obesity. However, none of the associations for PhenoAge or GrimAge reached statistical significance. The inconsistency across clocks may reflect the limitations of BMI as a measure of adiposity and has been observed in prior studies. Oblak et al. found positive correlations between BMI and epigenetic age for Horvath, Levine, and GrimAge clocks, but not for the Hannum clock [ 48 ]. More precise assessments of body composition—distinguishing subcutaneous from visceral fat and accounting for lean mass—could provide a clearer picture of how adiposity influences accelerated aging. Visceral fat is particularly harmful to metabolic function because it surrounds vital organs such as the liver, heart, and kidneys, while subcutaneous fat, though pro-inflammatory, may be less detrimental [ 56 , 57 ]. In contrast, greater lean mass is generally protective against aging and mortality [ 58 , 59 ].

Cardiometabolic diseases often occur together rather than in isolation, meaning that individuals classified with one condition are likely to meet criteria for others. To capture this clustering, we used metabolic syndrome, a composite risk score [ 18 ]. We observed consistent positive associations between metabolic syndrome and accelerated aging, particularly for DunedinPACE and GrimAge, but not PhenoAge. These findings align with prior studies suggesting that cumulative metabolic burden contributes to accelerated aging [ 48 ], although inconsistencies have also been reported [ 48 ]. However, after correction for multiple comparisons, the association between GrimAge and metabolic syndrome was no longer statistically significant, suggesting this finding should be interpreted cautiously. In a follow-up of the Berlin Aging Study, DunedinPACE predicted metabolic syndrome 7.4 years later [ 60 ].

Environmental factors also influence biological aging. Previous research has shown that poor early-life nutrition, such as famine exposure, is linked to an increased risk of diabetes and accelerated biological aging [ 61 ], indicating that early nutritional exposures can have lasting effects on metabolic and cellular processes. This cohort began as a community-randomized controlled trial designed to examine the impact of improved protein-energy nutrition on child growth and development. We have previously demonstrated that nutrition supplementation during the first 1,000 days of life (from conception to age 2) is associated with a lower risk of diabetes but paradoxically higher adiposity, which may reflect simultaneous improvements in human capital [ 13 , 14 ].

Most existing research, including this study, cannot fully determine the temporal relationships between early-life nutrition, diabetes, and accelerated aging [ 49 , 62 ]. It remains unclear whether poor early-life nutrition directly accelerates biological aging, thereby increasing disease risk, or whether it primarily influences disease risk through epigenetic programming or other pathways, which then affect the pace of aging. Our primary statistical model did not adjust for original intervention assignment; however, sensitivity analyses that did account for original treatment assignment showed slightly smaller effect sizes, while the direction and significance of associations remained consistent with the main model, suggesting that the early-life intervention does not meaningfully alter these associations.

Many studies report that men experience faster biological aging than women, but this pattern was not observed in our cohort [ 44 , 48 ]. Cardiometabolic disease was highly prevalent in our cohort and is known to accelerate aging. Women had a higher prevalence of each of the four cardiometabolic diseases we assessed (obesity, diabetes, hypertension and metabolic syndrome). This difference may reflect occupational or lifestyle factors, such as variations in physical activity. Consequently, the greater age acceleration observed among women contrasts with most previous studies, which generally report higher age acceleration in men.

Women in this cohort were also approaching menopause, and hormonal changes during this period can influence cardiometabolic disease risk, potentially contributing to this unexpected pattern [ 63 ]. Differences in how sex is incorporated into epigenetic clock construction may also help explain these findings. Sex was not explicitly included in the development of the PhenoAge clock [ 32 ], nor in the 19 biomarkers used to derive DunedinPACE [ 31 ]. While GrimAge does not explicitly include sex, it incorporates DNAm surrogates for smoking and mortality-related protein biomarkers that often differ by sex [ 38 ].

Interestingly, in sex-stratified analyses, the effect of diabetes on age acceleration was stronger in men than in women, despite women having a higher prevalence of diabetes. Although these analyses are underpowered, the differences may reflect disease severity in men or other risk factors, such as alcohol consumption or smoking, which were lower in women. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of considering both population-specific characteristics and clock-specific sensitivities when interpreting sex differences in biological aging.

Our study has several strengths. We leveraged data from a cluster-randomized trial of early-life nutritional supplementation with over five decades of follow-up and high participant retention. We also used reliable, standardized biomarkers to classify cardiometabolic diseases and collected DNA methylation data following established protocols. By generating established epigenetic clocks, we were able to estimate multiple measures of biological age, providing a comprehensive assessment of age acceleration in this well-characterized Guatemalan cohort.

Several limitations should also be considered. Our epigenetic age measures were collected at a single time point, which limits the ability to assess changes in biological aging over time and prevents determination of temporality between aging and disease. Furthermore, the epigenetic clocks applied were originally developed primarily in European-ancestry populations, which could introduce population-specific biases in a Hispanic/Latino cohort. While these clocks have shown generalizability across diverse populations, caution is warranted when interpreting absolute age estimates. Finally, we used the MethylationEPICv2 array, which lacks some CpG sites included in clocks developed on older arrays. Although established imputation and principal component correction methods were applied, this may affect direct comparability with other studies.

sections.conclusion: In summary, we observed biological age acceleration in this cohort of Guatemalan adults, particularly among women and individuals with diabetes. Longitudinal studies across varied settings are needed to clarify the causal relationships between epigenetic aging and cardiometabolic disease. A deeper understanding of the biological processes linking early-life exposures, aging, and disease will be critical for developing effective prevention and intervention strategies.
